Welbeck
WEL-bek
n. (the Nottinghamshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1153, head of the English circary, later a ducal palace)
Old English wella, a spring, and bec, a stream; the spring brook.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Welbeck in Nottinghamshire was founded in 1153 and became the head house of the Premonstratensian circary of England, its abbot visiting every other white-canon house in the country. It was surrendered in 1538 and granted away, and over the following centuries it became one of the great English country houses, seat of the dukes of Portland. The fifth duke, in the nineteenth century, spent a fortune excavating a system of tunnels, an underground ballroom and a subterranean library beneath the park, and lived almost entirely out of sight. This dictionary records Welbeck for the contrast between a house of canons and a buried palace, because Scripture addresses exactly this use of wealth. Haggai rebukes a people living in finished houses while God's house lies waste, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). A man who builds to hide himself is answered, “Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high” (Hab 2:9). A barn-building plan is interrupted, “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luk 12:20), and what we give was never ours, “all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a mansion as a dwelling house of considerable size; to excavate as to hollow out; wealth as large possessions; seclusion as separation from society; and ostentation as outward show to excite admiration.

expand to see more

MANSION, n. Any place of residence; a house; a habitation; particularly, the house of the lord of a manor.

EXCAVATE, v.t. To hollow; to cut, scoop, dig or wear out the inner part of any thing and make it hollow.

WEALTH, n. Riches; large possessions of money, goods or land; that abundance of worldly estate which exceeds the estate of the greater part of the community.

SECLUSION, n. The act of separating from society or connection; the state of being separate or apart; retirement; privacy.

OSTENTATION, n. Outward show or appearance; ambitious display; vain show, to excite admiration or to draw attention.

Key Scripture

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Hab 2:9 — "Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!"

Luk 12:20 — "But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?"

1Ch 29:14 — "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee."

Modern Corruption

Nottinghamshire Premonstratensian abbey of 1153, head of the English circary: surrendered in 1538 and turned into a ducal house with a tunnelled underworld.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Haggai's question, which was put to ordinary people rather than to a duke and which concerned priorities rather than architecture, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). Habakkuk adds the motive that Welbeck's tunnels make unusually literal: building in order to be out of reach, “that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil” (Hab 2:9).

The second thing is the interruption. The parable gives a man an excellent plan, adequate resources and no time, and the verdict is one word, “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luk 12:20). Against all of it stands David's prayer at the gathering of materials for the temple, which is the right posture of a rich man and is almost never the natural one, “for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew caphan (H5603), to cover or wainscot; Hebrew qen (H7064), a nest; Greek aphron (G878), a fool; Greek apaiteo (G523), to demand back; Hebrew betsa' (H1215), covetous gain.

expand to see more

Hebrew caphan (H5603) — to panel, to finish a house; “to dwell in your cieled houses”, Haggai 1:4.

Hebrew chareb (H2720) — waste, lying in ruin; “and this house lie waste”, Haggai 1:4.

Hebrew qen (H7064) — a nest, set out of reach; “that he may set his nest on high”, Habakkuk 2:9.

Greek aphron (G878) — senseless, a fool; “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee”, Luke 12:20.

Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, what was first received; “of thine own have we given thee”, 1 Chronicles 29:14.

Usage

"“to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4) — a question about priority, not architecture."

"“that he may set his nest on high” (Hab 2:9) — building in order to be out of reach."

"“of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14) — the posture a rich man almost never takes."
